title: Sonam Wangchuk Ends 26-Day Fast as India's Youth Protest Against Exam Leaks Grows
excerpt: The Ladakhi activist broke his hunger strike after negotiations with two federal ministers, but the Cockroach Janta Party movement vows to continue demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over NEET paper leaks.
body:
• Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on July 23 after negotiations with Union Ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, losing approximately 11 kg during the fast.
  • The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, which sparked the protests over NEET-UG exam paper leaks affecting 2 million students, says demonstrations will continue until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.
  • The protests have become the biggest youth-led challenge to PM Modi since 2014, spreading to cities across India and drawing support from Bollywood stars, opposition parties, and resident doctors' associations.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike on Friday after what he described as "a long negotiation on various conditions," but the youth movement that turned his fast into a nationwide flashpoint shows no sign of backing down.

Wangchuk, 59, broke his fast in the presence of Union Ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh at Medanta Hospital in Gurugram, where he had been undergoing treatment after being forcibly moved from his protest site at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on July 18. He said on X that scores of members of parliament had urged him to end the fast, and that concerns over "possible violence in the country" factored into his decision.

The NEET Paper Leak Crisis

At the heart of the protests are leaked question papers for the NEET-UG medical entrance exam, which affected an estimated 2 million students when they surfaced in May. The leaks are linked to several student suicides, according to Reuters, and have galvanized young Indians furious over what they see as systemic failures in the examination process.

The Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical movement founded by Abhijeet Dipke that began as online activism with just a few hundred participants — has grown into the largest youth-led challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government since he took office in 2014. Its central demand: the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

"We won't let Sonam sir's sacrifice go in vain."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

Dipke thanked Wangchuk for his "courage and sacrifice" but made clear the protests would continue until Pradhan steps down.

Escalation Across India

The movement has escalated sharply in recent days. On July 20, tens of thousands of people marched on parliament in a "Chalo Sansad" rally as the monsoon session opened. Police responded with tear gas and canes, and protesters have since alleged widespread police brutality. Delhi Police registered an FIR over an alleged assault on a Rapid Action Force officer during the clashes.

By Thursday, thousands had returned to Jantar Mantar carrying anti-government posters and chanting slogans. Authorities shut 16 Delhi Metro stations and ordered telecom companies to block mobile internet services in the area, disrupting digital payments for shops and restaurants in central Delhi. The New Delhi Traders Association asked all businesses in Connaught Place, the capital's bustling commercial hub, to close early.

Protests have spread beyond the capital to Ranchi, Pune, Thiruvananthapuram, and Kolkata, according to local media reports. Bollywood actors Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt, and Kareena Kapoor expressed support on social media, saying it was heartening to see students unite for a cause.

Modi's Response Falls Short

Prime Minister Modi on Thursday announced that special fast-track courts would be established to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks. "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!" he posted on X. He later said the government would announce stricter measures against paper leaks at a cabinet meeting on Friday.

CJP rejected the proposal. "But Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the first place?" spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said. "Fast-track courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues — you know the answer to that question, and so do we."

Pradhan, in his first public comments since demands for his resignation surfaced, said on Tuesday that the government was committed to addressing concerns and reforming exams. Opposition parties have echoed the movement's demands and disrupted the monsoon session of parliament.

From Ladakh to a National Symbol

Wangchuk began his fast on June 28 at Jantar Mantar. On his 21st day, Delhi Police forcibly moved him to Safdarjung Hospital after a court ordered health monitoring. His wife, Gitanjali Angmo, filed a petition alleging "illegal detention," and the Delhi High Court allowed his transfer to Medanta Hospital on July 21.

A Ladakhi education reformer and climate activist who won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2018, Wangchuk is widely believed to have inspired the lead character in a Bollywood blockbuster. He spent nearly six months in jail in 2025 after protests demanding statehood for Ladakh. His hunger strike over exam leaks won him a new following among Gen Z Indians, with supporters comparing him to Mahatma Gandhi — a comparison he has rejected.

"I am no Gandhi, no hero. I'm just an ordinary citizen who has not shied away from his responsibilities."

— Sonam Wangchuk

What's Next

After Wangchuk broke his fast, Modi urged him to follow doctors' advice and "regain weight lost." The activist promised to release a detailed video explaining the terms of the negotiations that led him to end the fast.

Nationwide demonstrations are planned for Friday in solidarity with students. The government has deployed 20 additional CRPF companies from West Bengal to Delhi — around 2,000 personnel airlifted from Kolkata. Human rights groups say the security measures, including metro shutdowns and internet blocks, amount to an attempt to stifle legitimate protest.

The CJP movement's trajectory — from a satirical online campaign to mass street protests backed by Bollywood, opposition parties, and medical professionals — suggests the crisis over exam integrity is far from over. For millions of Indian students, the issue of paper leaks remains a direct threat to their futures, and Pradhan's continued presence in the cabinet remains unacceptable.
nri_angle: The NEET exam crisis directly impacts Indian diaspora families whose children aspire to study medicine in India and raises questions about the credibility of Indian entrance examinations.
